sentences.t: We tend to admire people who can juggle several tasks at once.
Yet decades of research suggest that what we call multitasking is largely an illusion.
The brain does not actually perform two demanding activities simultaneously.
Instead, it switches rapidly between them, and every switch carries a hidden cost.
Psychologists refer to this as switching cost: the time and mental energy lost each time your attention shifts.
Individually, these losses are tiny, but they accumulate throughout the day.
The consequences go beyond mere inefficiency.
Frequent switching has been linked to more mistakes, shallower understanding, and a noticeable rise in stress.
Ironically, the people who consider themselves the best multitaskers often perform the worst, partly because they are the most easily distracted by anything new.
Many experts recommend working in focused blocks, typically between twenty-five and ninety minutes, with all notifications switched off.
Between blocks, take a genuine pause.
Stepping away allows the mind to consolidate what it has just processed.
It also helps to decide in advance what deserves your undivided attention, rather than letting the loudest demand dictate your priorities.
Ultimately, the goal is not to do more things at once, but to do the important things well.
And that begins with giving each task the attention it deserves.
